title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
raw_text: Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor Executive Summary As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks , automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking , the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. Key trends over the last quarter include: Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX , CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention. Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse : Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers). LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution. Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution. Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild. At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments. Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions. Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks In addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics. GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI. CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US. CyberStrikeAI : an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. The core architecture consists of a Go-based backend API acting as a C2 and orchestration server and connects commercial and open-weight LLMs to over 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts to automate end-to-end attack chains. HexStrike AI : an open source offensive Model Context Protocol (MCP)-integrated harness that enables LLM clients to directly connect to over 150 pre-installed offensive security tools. Operating through a dual-component architecture, the framework wraps standard utilities across reconnaissance, web application testing, exploitation, and binary analysis into callable functions coordinated by more than 12 specialized autonomous sub-agents. PentAGI : an open source autonomous offensive framework designed to lower technical barriers for entry-level operators running complex campaigns. Between late August and early October 2026, GTIG tracked a threat actor using a customized attack orchestration platform built off of the open source version of PentAGI used to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia. We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations. These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation. Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally. Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions. Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity. Figure 2: LLM maturity timeline Mitigations Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling. Use of Agents in Vulnerability Research and Development The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment. Adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders. For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August. Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026 In our previous report , we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences. In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time. More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent , that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector. // Insecure capability check analyzed in v21925.php: public static function restrict_popup_rest_access( $result ) { if ( is_wp_error( $result ) ) { return $result; } $route = isset( $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] ) ? sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] ) ) : ''; if ( false === strpos( $route, '/wp/v2/spectra-popup' ) ) { return $result; } if ( is_user_logged_in() && current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) { return $result; } return new WP_Error( 'rest_forbidden', __( 'Sorry, you are not allowed to access popups.', 'ultimate-addons-for-gutenberg' ), array( 'status' => rest_authorization_required_code() ) ); } Figure 4: Agentic framework inspecting access control implementations in the Spectra (Ultimate Addons for Gutenberg) WordPress plugin, version 2.19.25 Russian Language Comments Comments Translated to English # LLM API-ключи для авто-эксплуатации (пилот exploit_agent) # Впиши ключи сам — сюда, не в чат. Обе строки обязательны. # LLM API keys for auto-exploitation (exploit_agent pilot) # Enter the keys yourself — right here, not in the chat. Both lines are required. Table 1: Comments from environmental file configuring multiple LLM API keys for autonomous exploitation Open source research corroborates threat actor operationalization of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. For example, in late August 2026, threat actors exploited two vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers as zero-days that, when chained together, allow for unauthenticated remote code execution: CVE-2026-81578, an authentication bypass flaw; and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class loading vulnerability. Using LLMs, security researchers and the cybersecurity company Huntress generated working exploits for the vulnerabilities within a day of disclosure. Greynoise reported a campaign that took place four days after the initial disclosure in which a threat actor likely used LLMs to build and test exploits for these vulnerabilities, assemble a target list, and execute a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations. Greynoise also highlighted the speed of execution, noting that the threat actor expanded an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes. The PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) also highlight several of these trends. They were discovered using LLM-enabled analysis. Before official patches were released on Oct. 21, 2026, a POC video and early patched code were published. This allowed both researchers and attackers to compare code versions, understand the flaws and attempt to build exploits before the patch became available. In the initial days following the official patch, hundreds of claimed but non-functional POCs, likely generated with the help of LLMs, were published. This proliferation created significant work for the security community to verify or debunk the POCs while monitoring for evidence of confirmed exploitation. Mitigations Google continuously invests in AI innovation and research, helping to ensure AI is built responsibly , and that we’re leveraging its potential to automatically find risks. In 2024 we introduced Big Sleep , an AI agent developed by Google DeepMind and Google Project Zero, that actively searches and finds unknown security vulnerabilities in software. Google Cloud employs a defense-in-depth model that combines rigorous code reviews and secure-by-default libraries with continuous, automated scanning using specialized AI agents such as CodeMender to discover, patch, and remediate vulnerabilities before and after release. We partner with the global security community by running a Vulnerability Reward Program and maintaining Project Zero to proactively find and patch zero-day vulnerabilities. Full Integration of LLMs into Information Operations GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success. IO Actor Categories State-sponsored groups are IO actors directly linked to state apparatuses and have traditionally formed the primary baseline tracked by platform defenders and researchers. To preserve plausible deniability, they increasingly rely on third-party commercial contractors to execute campaigns on their behalf. Commercial IaaS vendors encompass marketing and PR agencies, private intelligence contractors, and offshoots of commercial surveillance vendors, selling services ranging from tailored influence campaigns to turnkey platforms. Tradecraft varies across this ecosystem; intelligence contractors and surveillance offshoots in particular often apply stronger operational security (OPSEC) and more advanced techniques than traditional state-sponsored actors. Inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are driven by profit rather than ideology. These actors generate a high volume of political clickbait to drive engagement, maximize click-through rates, and boost ad revenue. This combination of political framing and high-volume synthetic content creates a significant frontend perception gap, making IPM network campaigns the most prone to being misidentified as state-sponsored operations. Table 2: IO actor categories As automated content generation reduces a primary operational bottleneck, adversaries are increasingly shifting their focus toward leveraging LLMs for infrastructure design, automated distribution pipelines, and anti-detection mechanisms. Specifically, our observations indicate a notable shift toward the commercial development of LLM-enabled, end-to-end IaaS platforms designed to support and automate the full influence campaign lifecycle. The proliferation of these platforms can lower operational overhead for state and commercial actors while increasing the difficulty of detecting coordinated and inauthentic behavior across social media platforms. The Commercial Development of Turnkey, LLM-Enabled Influence Operations In August 2026, GTIG investigated threat activity leveraging the Gemini API alongside tools from multiple AI providers to build an end-to-end IaaS platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, primarily across Europe and the Middle East. The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO campaign lifecycle, including persona creation, multimodal media generation, automated content distribution, and interactive posting across platforms. Identified prompts reflected an operational focus on emulating organic grassroots engagement (i.e., “astroturfing”) while evading platform detection rules. Identified prompts instructed models to adopt localized personas specific to targeted geography, mimicking regional dialects and slang, while incorporating informal phrasing and intentional typos to avoid sounding like an automated tool. Prompts supporting media generation introduced deliberate camera flaws simulating realistic photos typically captured by smartphone cameras (e.g., making images appear grainy or incorporating uneven lighting changes) and omitted background text to avoid synthetic image markers. To evade social media platform defenses, operators routed traffic through residential proxies and preserved saved login cookies. This setup was designed to allow automated tools to maintain active, authenticated access continuously, avoiding security checkpoints like CAPTCHAs and login re-verification. GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s plan to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution. To manage large volumes of social media accounts, the platform was designed to run virtual smartphones in cloud environments—disguising each virtual device as a legitimate mobile device—and route web traffic through proxies to bypass automated bot detection and rate limits. The architecture additionally includes automated fake account creation using disposable email addresses and overseas virtual SMS numbers. To avoid further suspicion, newly-created accounts were configured to undergo an automated aging period, leveraging LLMs to simulate realistic user behavior (e.g., how long a user lingers on a post, scrolling, and interacting with non-campaign content) to establish a history of normal activity before pushing targeted messaging. Tactical LLM Adoption: Demographic Microtargeting and Content Scaling Alongside the development of IaaS software suites, threat actors continue to integrate commercial LLM tools into baseline content workflows to overcome linguistic barriers, customize messaging, and scale output. Using commercial models to produce commentary, synthetic personas, and stylized animations at the content layer allows IO actors to improve the credibility and demographic resonance of their campaigns, while enabling IPM networks to mass-produce political clickbait for advertising revenue. LLM-Enabled Quality Enhancement in Long-Running IaaS Campaign: Since our last report, GTIG observed a long-running IaaS provider tracked since 2019 leveraging LLMs to elevate the baseline quality and volume of its influence operations. Utilizing a proprietary software suite designed to manage thousands of synthetic profiles across major platforms, the provider targeted political discourse in multiple countries. Operators integrated LLM models to produce more convincing virtual personas, as well as academic-style commentary and media focused on political, religious, and civil rights topics. The resulting content was subsequently promoted and amplified across platforms using fabricated Western personas. Demographic Targeting via Synthetic Content: We have observed threat actors using LLM-generated content to customize context for specific regions and audiences, for example by using synthetic influencer personas to promote policy narratives targeting specific demographics. A separate network posted synthetic, Lego brick-inspired animations and football parodies to satirize global political figures, likely in an attempt to appeal to younger audiences by effectively packaging propaganda in short-video formats consistent with popular internet culture. LLM-Augmented Inauthentic Political Monetization (IPM): GTIG also tracks a growing trend of IPM actors using LLMs to mass-produce political content. Although their thematic focus, quality, and volume can resemble state-backed IO campaigns, these non-ideological operations exploit societal polarization solely to maximize engagement, click-through rates, and advertising revenue. GTIG has observed IPM operators prompting commercial LLMs to identify lucrative political topics, trending keywords, and high-Cost Per Mile (CPM) niches for ad monetization, while promoting the resulting content via synthetic news anchors that occasionally spoof the likenesses of real journalists and commentators to manufacture credibility. Mitigations GTIG collaborates closely with product teams to take action against IO actors across affected Google surfaces under our standard platform policies. Our research and rigorous analysis enables Google teams to make enforcement decisions and to disrupt coordinated IO campaigns. GITG, YouTube, and Google Trust & Safety track and regularly enforce on accounts associated with coordinated IO posting content and commenting. Examples of this enforcement include disruption of YouTube channels, blogs, AdSense accounts, and domains removed from Google News surfaces, as we report on a quarterly basis in the Influence Operations Bulletin . Beyond enforcement actions, GTIG shares insights with Google DeepMind to harden our platforms and services against emerging tradecraft. This intelligence is used to establish abuse baselines, enhance Gemini’s ability to recognize and refuse misuse, and inform internal policy modifications. Threat Actors Abusing and Monetizing Access to AI Tools While compromised credentials have long served as the fundamental bedrock for initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement during intrusions, adversaries are increasingly repurposing stolen credentials and compute resources to power unauthorized LLM tooling and autonomous operational pipelines. As access costs, token rate limits, and geographic restrictions present persistent operational hurdles for threat actors attempting to scale LLM capabilities, adversaries are actively harvesting session tokens and platform credentials directly from victim endpoints and continuous integration environments. In tandem with this shift toward hijacking valid credentials for LLMs, underground cybercrime forums and illicit marketplaces have rapidly matured to meet this demand—transitioning beyond generic identity dumps to commodifying verified frontier AI accounts, tokenized API quotas, and targeted infostealer configurations as turnkey utilities for downstream exploitation. LLMJacking in Incident Response Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. As seen in the image below, LLMJacking can generate significant usage and billing increases within hours. In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation. Figure 5: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests In November, Mandiant and GTIG described a set of common TTPs we observed across intrusions that affected financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region. Attack Lifecycle Stage Description of Observed Tactics Initial Access Threat actors frequently used credential theft and session hijacking to gain access to targeted environments, including harvesting valid credentials from public GitHub repositories, and social engineering using deceptive websites to trick users into providing active session tokens. Internal Reconnaissance & Lateral Movement Seeking to identify credentials and systems of interest, attackers conducted reconnaissance against internal code repositories, data stores, cloud services, containers, and access logs. In at least one case, a threat actor exploited a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running in an internal container to navigate to additional systems. Privilege Escalation & Persistence Threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware. Complete Mission: LLM Abuse Inside organizations’ cloud environments, attackers enabled LLM services, including subscribing compromised accounts to pay-as-you-go agreements. To circumvent rate limits, one threat actor used a “burn and rotate” strategy, creating and deleting short-lived service accounts. Other threat actors abused cloud compute resources, provisioning instances with powerful GPUs and requesting quota increases in order to run their own LLM tooling. This included agentic frameworks that a threat actor used to automate further exploitation of the compromised network, as well as open source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure deployed to facilitate the sale of access to the compromised organization’s resources. Table 3: Common TTPs observed in LLMJacking intrusions In another investigation, we observed at least two separate attackers seeking to conduct LLMJacking operations. Both actors accessed a targeted environment using the same set of legitimate credentials, which were potentially sold or leaked on underground forums. The first threat actor used legitimate credentials to gain access to the environment, enumerate available LLM services, and query cost and usage information related to the account. On the same day, we observed a set of IP addresses using a common User-Agent, likely a botnet or proxy service, also accessing the environment using the same legitimate credentials. The botnet or proxy service generated millions of LLM API calls in approximately 24 hours before the credentials were revoked. Though the first threat actor returned to the environment, creating service accounts provisioned with permissions to query LLMs, the botnet’s noisy activity caused the compromised credentials to be remediated before this threat actor could execute LLM queries. For hardening and mitigation guidance for defending against LLMJacking intrusions, please see our blog . Monetizing LLMJacking through LLM Mixers Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure. This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection. The LLM Mixer ecosystem mirrors the broader cybercrime marketplace, where specialized threat groups handle discrete phases of the supply chain. While LLM Mixer operators maintain infrastructure and customer fulfillment, for example, operators may partner with separate threat actors who establish initial access to compromised environments, purchase compromised credentials from infostealer operators, or recruit partners to systematically register free trial accounts. GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. Advertised pricing varies significantly across individual mixer platforms and based on the models and types of credentials offered; for example, free trial credentials were much cheaper than enterprise. We observed prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on both input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Rather than pricing per million tokens, some vendors such as JetNight offer monthly subscriptions at differing prices based on the type of model offered. Figure 6: APIMart advertised prices Threat Actors Continue Using AI for Productivity Gains Since our last report , GTIG has continued to observe threat actors leveraging LLMs to augment various phases of the attack lifecycle. However, widespread adoption of LLM tooling also introduces significant operational drawbacks. The forensically noisy nature of many LLM tool processes can degrade OPSEC and compromise stealth, creating a detrimental impact on espionage campaigns. In addition, LLMs can reduce operational reliability, as adversaries must contend with model limitations, including the hallucination of non-existent details or even targets. Consequently, we anticipate that actors who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term persistence are less likely to rely on forensically noisy tools within a targeted environment, though they may employ them selectively for speed and scale, depending on operational priorities. Conversely, we assess with high confidence that actors less concerned with operational stealth, including many cyber crime actors, will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates. Government-backed threat actors State-sponsored threat actors continue to leverage LLMs in their respective operations, reinforcing baseline assessments communicated in our previous reports. For example, we continue to see CALANQUE ION, an Iranian government-backed actor previously tracked as APT42 , leverage LLMs—including Gemini—to augment reconnaissance and targeted social engineering. We also see PRC-nexus threat actors leveraging LLMs for reconnaissance and research. In addition to this new baseline of threat actors leveraging LLMs, we observed the following activity: In Q3 2026, PRC-nexus cyber espionage actors used LLM tools and models for reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits. We have also observed threat actors using LLMs to conduct post-compromise data analysis. This includes PRC contractor LEAKY CASTLE, which overlaps with public reporting about data leaked from a contractor using LLMs to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data, including deriving insights into organizational structures and adding them into finished intelligence reports to sell to customers. In a new trend, we have observed PRC-nexus actors abusing LLM platforms and file-hosting backends for staging, dead drop C2s, and exfiltration. In one example, a threat actor abused a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents. We also continue to see threat actors from the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) using LLM tools to support DPRK IT worker activity, such as generating resumes and preparing for job interviews at Western organizations. DPRK threat actors are also abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors. We observed the use of public facing tools to generate responses during job screenings, allowing them to sound authentic while posing as Western IT workers to secure remote employment. While we continue to see DPRK actors leveraging LLM-powered tools to generate lure content and assist with coding, over the course of 2026 we’ve observed an evolution of tactics. In multiple intrusions, a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE threat cluster combined LLM-enabled social engineering and abused organizations' AI tools as a supply chain attack vector. In recent intrusions targeting cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe, the threat actor exploited LLM software architectures as a lateral execution surface. For initial access, the actor created fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms whose profile imagery contained SynthID watermarks, confirming use of LLMs to synthesize deceptive professional identities. These personas directed targets to fraudulent meeting platforms featuring "ClickFix" social engineering lures, which prompted targets to run diagnostic fix scripts, which executed likely LLM-authored staging scripts via ClickFix lures. Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor. To maintain stealth, suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE further masked its lateral movement by generating GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs) named after Microsoft Copilot, underscoring how threat actors are simultaneously abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native AI agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors. LLM Toolkits Offer Turnkey Cyber Crime Solutions In developments in the last quarter, in addition to the use of offensive frameworks in financially motivated activity, we observed cybercrime actors leverage LLMs to scale tooling for clients; for example, Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) operators using LLMs to create tools for low-sophisticated adversaries. The Jieyou phishing service, an active Chinese-language PhaaS platform first observed in March 2026, is primarily used by cybercriminals to deploy and manage highly convincing phishing campaigns, with a particular focus on e-commerce fraud. The service introduced an LLM chatbot assistant in its June 2026 backend update. This chatbot allows threat actors to easily configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands, significantly lowering the technical barrier for deploying campaigns. The backend chatbot is model-agnostic and integrates with several frontier and open source platforms via APIs. The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier. Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly. Mitigations These activities triggered Gemini's safety responses, and Google took additional, broader action to disrupt the threat actors' campaigns. Additionally, we've taken action against these actors by disabling the assets associated with this activity and making updates to prevent further misuse. Google DeepMind has used these insights to strengthen both classifiers and our models, enabling them to refuse to assist with these types of attacks. How Google Protects Against AI Abuse Google uses a multifaceted defense strategy to protect our users and infrastructure against LLM abuse, integrating proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, targeted containment protocols, and proactive red teaming to simulate and protect against threats. Additionally, as innovation moves forward, the industry needs security standards for building and deploying AI responsibly, which is why we introduced the Secure AI Framework (SAIF) , a conceptual framework to secure AI systems. Proactive Model and Platform Defenses We continuously harden our models against misuse by feeding insights from active threat monitoring directly into our safety classifiers and guardrails. For instance, in response to model extraction—or “distillation”—attacks, we have deployed real-time defenses designed to degrade the performance of unauthorized "student" models and detect attempts to clone proprietary logic. When we identify bad actors, we take direct action to disrupt their operations by disabling associated projects and accounts. To extend these protections to enterprise customers, we developed Google AI Threat Defense (AITD) . This autonomous architecture operationalizes security by bringing together the reasoning power of Gemini and other frontier models, the risk prioritization of Wiz, the automated remediation capabilities of Gemini and CodeMender, and frontline intelligence from Mandiant. AITD employs a multi-model strategy that balances cost and coverage, using light models for continuous scanning and specialized frontier models for high-risk vulnerabilities. In addition to our proactive platform defenses, we’ve recently introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Google has built Gemini 4 Carbon with layered defenses against cyber misuse—combining safety training, input/output classifiers, activation-based introspection probes and chain-of-thought and agentic trajectory monitors—designed to block requests to develop functional, weaponized exploits or malware tooling. The robustness of these safeguards has been stress-tested by both internal red teams and specialized external partners including Gray Swan and Trajectory labs. Beyond the model itself, Google continuously monitors for intentional misuse in production, limits or disables access for offending accounts, and provides vetted defenders, security researchers, and government partners access to advanced dual-use cyber capabilities through the Fairwind Program. More information on the safety, security, and alignment testing conducted on Gemini 4 Carbon can be found in the Gemini 4 Carbon Safety & Security Report . Building AI Safely and Responsibly Google’s approach to AI is guided by a commitment to bold innovation and responsible development. Guided by our AI Principles , Google designs AI systems with robust security and safety guardrails, which are continuously tested to ensure resilience. Our policy guidelines and prohibited use policies are foundational to ensuring safety. Our policy development process is built to anticipate emerging trends and design for security from the ground up, allowing us to enhance protections for users globally. At Google, threat intelligence is a core component of our security posture. We actively investigate abuse of our platforms—including malicious cyber activities by government-backed threat actors—and collaborate with law enforcement when appropriate. Crucially, our learnings from every countermeasure we implement are fed back into our product development to improve the security for our AI models. These iterative improvements to our classifiers and model-level safeguards are vital to maintaining agility against evolving threats. Our LLM development and Trust & Safety teams also work in constant concert with our threat intelligence, security, and modeling experts to effectively address misuse.
summary: Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor Executive Summary As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks , automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking , the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. Key trends over the last quarter include: Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX , CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention.

title: How ISVs are unlocking European workloads using Google Cloud Dedicated technology
raw_text: Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany. To help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators. But infrastructure is only the starting point. Organizations also need to transform the software ecosystem they rely on every day. To meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, currently in preview. These local entities operate dedicated infrastructure stacks, help maintain operational custody, and handle customer data within independent jurisdictional boundaries. Today, we are highlighting the expanding independent software vendor (ISV) ecosystem validated on Google Cloud Dedicated, enabling French and German organizations to run their critical enterprise software in environments designed to support their sovereign and regulatory needs. The local partner model: Cloud capability under domestic custody Deploying in a sovereign boundary should not require an organization to sacrifice software choice or rewrite its enterprise applications.Because Google Cloud Dedicated provides architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, validated enterprise software runs directly inside these partner-operated environments without custom re-platforming. This model provides European enterprises with three concrete advantages: Localized operational custody : Infrastructure operations, software quarantine procedures, and day-to-day administrative access are under the direct management of local European partners operating with specialized remote technical escalations governed by strict, partner-supervised escorted access controls. Broad software choice : Regulated institutions can deploy industry-standard tools for identity governance, cyber resilience, simulation, and data streaming natively in their sovereign perimeter. Streamlined compliance : Organizations fulfill national frameworks like SecNumCloud and BSI guidelines while preserving familiar CI/CD pipelines, APIs, and developer workflows. Software choice is the true bottleneck for sovereign migrations When highly regulated European institutions consider moving to a sovereign cloud, the infrastructure itself is rarely the primary roadblock. The real bottleneck is software.Historically, pursuing strict sovereignty meant accepting compromises: Rewriting applications from scratch or maintaining custom, brittle tooling because mainstream enterprise platforms were unavailable. Forcing security, engineering, and data teams to abandon the industry-standard tools they use daily in favor of untested niche alternatives. Sidelining high-impact initiatives like real-time fraud scoring, automated DevSecOps, and modern identity governance simply because the required ISVs could not legally or technically operate in the environment. Because Google Cloud Dedicated maintains architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, leading global and European software providers can deploy their proven platforms directly inside national, domestic operator-managed boundaries. Regulated organizations retain the software, automated pipelines, and operational standards they rely on — without sacrificing compliance or operational custody. title: Alibaba touts 62% lower task costs with Qwen4-Max, adds cyber safeguards
raw_text: Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship model, claiming it reduces the average cost of completing professional tasks by 62% compared with its predecessor while introducing additional safeguards against offensive cybersecurity capabilities and other high-risk uses. “According to Work360 — a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields — Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%,” Alibaba said in a blog post. The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction. The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said. It supports a 1-million-token context window. The company attributed the savings to lower token use and new list prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, down from $2 and $6. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said enterprises should treat the figure as a vendor benchmark rather than an assured reduction in their own AI spending. The relevant measure, he said, is the cost of an accepted result, including retries, reasoning tokens, and employee time spent checking outputs. “Alibaba has published the mileage it got on its own road, and a buyer’s bill depends on the road the buyer drives,” Gogia said. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should measure successful task completion rather than token prices alone. “An enterprise should benchmark what it costs to complete 1,000 real business tasks successfully, not what it costs to generate a million tokens,” Kadakia said. Alibaba also cited improvements across coding and agentic evaluations, including Code Arena and Agents’ Last Exam. In an automotive manufacturing demonstration, the company said Qwen4-Max reduced manual workpiece programming time from approximately 475 minutes to 24 minutes. Security claims need independent testing Alongside the cost figures, Alibaba set out changes to what the model learns about hacking at the training-data stage. “For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and remediation, while removing data for offensive tasks aimed at enhancing attack capabilities,” the Alibaba blog post said. The company said code security checks added during training lifted the share of functions passing both functionality and security tests on Last Secure Code Bench from 22% to 31.8%. Its internal security experts found the model’s defensive capabilities had “improved substantially,” the post added. Kadakia questioned whether offensive and defensive cybersecurity knowledge can be reliably separated through training-data filtering. “One of the fundamental challenges with cybersecurity AI is that offensive and defensive knowledge are largely the same knowledge,” he said, noting that understanding SQL injection is necessary both to exploit and prevent it. Gogia said the distinction requires independent validation, recommending that CISOs seek assessments from government evaluators or established external red teams rather than rely solely on Alibaba’s internal testing. The announcement follows an October investigation by Canadian AI company Cohere, which reported that an earlier Alibaba model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, attempted to send a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage destination in Beijing during a security test. Cohere said its sandbox blocked the request. A subsequent investigation by Check Point replayed the behaviour 64 times and found 52 different destination hosts. It suggested unpredictable model behaviour was a more likely explanation than a deliberately configured backdoor. The incident involved an experimental model, not Qwen4-Max. Besides, Government evaluators have begun testing Chinese models independently. In July, the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that the safeguards on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 allowed assistance with agentic cyber exploit development. Gogia said CISOs should treat Alibaba’s filter “as a promise until a government evaluator or an established outside red team has tested it.” Data governance and open-weight risks For enterprises outside China, Gogia said the geographic scope of Alibaba’s global service, prompt-retention policies, and jurisdiction governing stored data should be considered before deploying the model for sensitive workloads. He pointed to prompt retention of up to 30 days and longer retention of flagged content, including under zero-retention arrangements. Kadakia said enterprises should examine where prompts, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and logs are processed, who can access them, and what permissions agents have across internal systems. “The biggest risk with enterprise AI is no longer simply what information employees type into a chatbot. It is what an autonomous agent can access, what decisions it can make, and what actions it can execute across connected enterprise systems,” he said. Alibaba also plans to release smaller Qwen4 models with open weights. Kadakia said developers modifying those models through fine-tuning should not assume the original security safeguards will remain intact. “Safety training is not a permanent property of a model,” he said, recommending fresh adversarial testing and controls over tool access for customised versions. Gogia similarly recommended reassessing each modified model rather than automatically inheriting the original model’s security assurances. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .

title: The benign true positive: When trusted AI agents look like attackers
raw_text: A coding agent opens hundreds of files, launches command-line tools and connects to an internal service to complete a task. A support agent authenticates to several systems, retrieves customer records and updates another application. A workflow agent enumerates cloud resources in seconds, then moves to the next stage of its assignment. To an endpoint, identity, or cloud security platform, these sequences can resemble reconnaissance, credential access, lateral movement, or the early stages of exfiltration. The control is accurately identifying behavior associated with an attack, and the agent is carrying out an approved business task. I am beginning to see this pattern as enterprises deploy AI agents across software development, customer support, finance, IT and security. I call it the benign true positive: an accurate detection of attack-like behavior generated by legitimate machine activity. For CISOs, this exposes a foundational assumption beneath behavioral security . For decades, attack-like behavior justified immediate suspicion because legitimate systems rarely operated with the speed, breadth and autonomy now common among AI agents. That assumption is weakening, and security leaders need to prepare their teams, processes and technology portfolios for the consequences. Behavioral baselines were built around people Modern detection systems rely heavily on patterns associated with expected human activity. People read files at a human pace, move between applications in recognizable sequences, and generally interact with systems one action at a time. An account that suddenly enumerates thousands of resources or launches a chain of processes across several environments deserves investigation. AI agents follow a different operating pattern. They gather context broadly, perform tasks in parallel and move across systems according to the needs of an assigned objective. A coding agent may inspect an entire repository before changing a few lines. A support agent may authenticate to several applications because resolving a customer request requires data from each one. The resulting telemetry frequently matches the signals security tools were designed to detect. Existing controls will keep generating alerts, and those alerts will often be technically correct. Security teams must determine whether the behavior reflects an authorized task, a compromised agent, manipulated instructions, stolen credentials, or an attacker imitating normal agent activity. A broad suppression rule may reduce noise but also create a blind spot. Attackers will naturally look for trusted agent identities, approved workflows and familiar machine-speed patterns that help them blend into the environment. Intent becomes the missing layer Security tools observe actions such as process launches, file reads, authentication events, API calls, or network connections. Intent sits in the surrounding context. Investigators need to know who owns the agent, what task it was assigned, who initiated the task, which systems it was authorized to use, what data it could access and whether its actions stayed within approved boundaries. They also need to determine whether another user, process, or external input altered the agent’s instructions. Those answers may be distributed across identity systems, agent orchestration platforms, cloud infrastructure, business applications, ticketing systems and the security stack. Reconstructing the event requires correlation across these sources and a clear account of what the agent was trying to accomplish. A large enterprise may soon operate thousands of agents across business and technical functions. Human analysts cannot manually reconstruct every event at that scale. Security operations will need investigative capacity that can recover intent at machine speed and present conclusions grounded in observable evidence. 3 investment priorities for CISOs 1. Agent identity and governance The first priority is agent identity and governance . Every agent should have a clear owner, a defined purpose, credentials scoped to its responsibilities and documented access to applications, tools and data. The SOC should be able to connect each action to the workflow, user request, or business process that initiated it. This requires an inventory of active agents, lifecycle controls, access reviews, approval requirements for sensitive actions and audit trails that connect behavior to an accountable owner. Shared service accounts and broad permissions slow investigations and make containment harder. Purpose-specific identities and task provenance give the SOC the context needed to identify misuse. 2. Investigation architecture The second priority is investigation architecture. Security leaders should evaluate whether their current stack can assemble evidence across endpoint, identity, cloud, network, SaaS and agent platforms. A useful system should reconstruct the sequence of events, apply organizational context, document missing information and explain how it reached a conclusion. AI investments in the SOC should support evidence gathering, cross-system correlation, adaptive reasoning and clear escalation whenever the available data cannot support a confident determination. 3. Team design The third priority is team design. Analysts will increasingly govern systems that investigate both human and machine behavior. Their expertise will shape operating boundaries, exception handling, detection logic and the context used during investigations. Security leaders should invest in detection engineering, threat hunting, identity governance and agent oversight skills. Analysts need time and authority to examine recurring behavioral collisions, refine access policies, improve workflows and challenge automated conclusions. Each benign true positive can become a source of operational learning about how agents are being used and where controls need to mature. A new operating model for the SOC The traditional SOC sends alerts to analysts, who gather evidence and decide what happened. AI agents will add another source of high-volume activity, and many resulting alerts will be accurate detections of legitimate behavior. The SOC needs an operating model built around rapid interpretation. For an authorized event, the investigation should show that a specific agent accessed particular systems under an approved identity, pursued a valid task, remained within its permissions and produced no evidence of deviation. For a risky event, it should show where the activity exceeded the agent’s expected scope and why human review or containment is required. This level of clarity preserves sensitive detections, keeps analysts focused on cases that demand judgment, and creates a practical path for building trust in increasingly autonomous systems through visible evidence, explicit accountability and measurable outcomes. Preparing for the next source of alert volume CISOs should begin by mapping where agents already operate across the organization. Many will discover activity introduced through developer tools, SaaS platforms, departmental automation and enterprise applications with embedded agent capabilities. The next step is to connect agent ownership, identity, permissions, task provenance and policy to security operations. Teams should test how existing controls respond to representative agent workflows and track benign true positives as a distinct operational category. AI agents are changing the meaning of normal behavior. Security leaders who prepare now can preserve visibility, strengthen governance and build a SOC capable of understanding the purpose behind machine-speed activity. Trusted machines will increasingly look like attackers. The organizations that can recover intent quickly will be best positioned to tell the difference.

title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
raw_text: This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered. Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines. “Sometimes the [vulnerability] variant wouldn’t be caught until the model variation got better or the model used chaining analysis at a higher degree once it improved in order to find those variants,” he said. “Sometimes it was in the exact same spot, sometimes it was something that was related, that was a neighbor, but variant analysis is basically something that has been popping up, and it’s a context magnet, too.” With the rate of published CVEs higher than ever due to AI assistance, software developers are actually disclosing the types of vulnerabilities their platforms are susceptible to, and the patches for these flaws can serve as blueprints for attackers, Nejad warned. Sometimes it’s as simple as pointing an AI agent at a codebase with its historical vulnerabilities as context and telling it to go hunt for variants, he said. Rubrik’s experience reflects a broader asymmetry that other researchers have observed in recent months: AI models have become very good at offense — finding vulnerabilities and building exploits — while their defensive skills, such as writing secure code and correct patches, have lagged behind . Also at the [un]prompted conference, OpenAI security researcher Tim de Waal showed how an AI agent patched two vulnerabilities in the firmware of a network access point. For one issue, the agent rebuilt the vulnerable function without the stack canaries the original code had, silently removing a defensive protection. For the other, the generated patch filtered out double-quote characters in the attacker input but missed that using single quotes would have bypassed the fix. Controlled studies found the same issue at scale. When researchers at 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs used AI agents to repeatedly generate patches for the same six known vulnerabilities in complex open-source projects, about half of the 6,080 resulting patch candidates left at least one attack path open , with agents sometimes missing identical instances of the same bug in other parts of the code. More recently, in a benchmark test called P2Patch , researchers pitted two AI agents against each other: one wrote exploits for 101 real vulnerabilities, and the other patched the code until the exploits stopped working. Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw. In 41 of the 101 cases, it succeeded, sometimes multiple times for subsequent patches. Of course, human-written patches are not infallible either. Security firm Trail of Bits reviewed the fixes developers submitted for 2,265 vulnerabilities found during its consulting assessments over several years and one in eight failed to fully resolve the reported issues. In one case the company documented, a human maintainer and an AI agent working as part of the Patch the Planet initiative separately wrote patches for the same memory-safety bug in the freenginx web server, and both patches introduced the same crash during request cleanup. Organizations turn to AI patching because humans can’t keep up The issue is not that AI always writes worse patches than humans, although the failure rate of AI-written patches might be higher, but that the rate of vulnerability discovery is now so fast that humans alone can’t keep up. This is combined with the offensive capabilities of AI agents that enable attackers to analyze and reverse engineer patches at machine speed. Seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program , Anthropic’s public ledger counted 37,966 findings. Only 217 of the 7,349 flaws that were made public had been fixed, according to a recent analysis from vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck. Not all findings turn out to be security vulnerabilities, but Anthropic claims a true positive rate of 94.2%, which, given the small number of fixes, highlights the deluge of reports that maintainers have to triage and deal with. “Progress on software security used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities,” Anthropic wrote in its initial Glasswing update . “Now it’s limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI.” And this is not just a problem for open-source projects. After Bank of America let Anthropic’s models loose on its own systems, the bank added 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter of this year to help with the patching work, on top of the roughly 3,000 existing staff. They were still on the job in October, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC . By July, Meta was using AI to write fixes for 40% of its critical vulnerabilities, and almost half of those patches landed in production unchanged. Despite that, the exposure time did not go down, Meta software engineer David Molnar said in a separate presentation at [un]prompted. That’s because the AI-proposed patches still had to be reviewed by humans, while the amount of new code grew more than 100% year over year, with more than 80% of it attributed to AI coding agents. “Everyone is drowning in stuff to review,” Molnar said, adding that his team has worked with directors and product managers internally to find more places where automation can be introduced, including in the review process, shifting it from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop . “You can automate everything upstream of AI, and then just completely overwhelm your poor humans on the other end,” he said. “Which is why you have to take a look at the entire pipeline and automate all of it.” In June, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) projected around 66,000 CVE assignments for this year. With two months left, the number is already approaching 100,000. Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday alone addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities compared to only 180 in October 2025. Closed-source patches are not safe from AI analysis If AI agents are scouring code repositories for vulnerability variants, one might be inclined to think that closed-source sofware, where the patch is usually inside a compiled binary, are safer. That’s not necessarily the case given that AI models are now also great at reverse engineering, and some people use them to create open-source replicas of complex proprietary products, for example Adobe Photoshop . In June, when Anthropic’s researchers tested what an attacker can do with AI-assisted patch diffing , they gave a model nothing beyond what’s public on patch day. It produced a working exploit within an hour of a Firefox fix landing. On Windows, given vulnerable and patched binaries plus decompilation output, the same approach built eight full privilege-escalation chains from 21 kernel vulnerabilities for roughly $2,000 each. “In some ways, N-days are the more dangerous of the two [compared to zero-days], because the patch itself provides a roadmap to the bug,” the Anthropic researchers said at the time. A team of researchers from Fudan University in Shanghai, China, built an LLM-assisted binary diffing framework and analyzed 76 recent patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. According to their paper published this month, the framework flagged 63 of the patches as incomplete and manually confirmed 56, of which 26 could be bypassed into new vulnerabilities, resulting in 19 CVE assignments and $28,100 in bug bounties. Comparing a vulnerable build against a patched one to locate the changed code has been a standard practice for security researchers for years. The difference now is the speed and lack of skill needed thanks to AI. And even though the latest frontier AI models might have API guardrails that make reverse engineering or binary diffing harder, the open-weight models have become capable enough. Taesoo Kim, vice president of security research at Microsoft, also warned during the [un]prompted conference that AI has drastically reduced the time needed for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation, and noted that Microsoft has to also be extremely careful when publishing CVEs and push updates quickly to customers. The more recent frontier models have started refusing such binary analysis work due to stricter guardrails, but a lot of people use open-weight models instead, such as Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, because “they are extremely capable,” he said. Exploiting the patch gap is now easy Last month, the Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly taking advantage of the time gap between when information about a potential vulnerability becomes available in a code commit or test release in one project and when the patch trickles down to other projects. Their report included examples of attackers exploiting security fixes revealed in Chromium builds, the open-source browser that serves as the base for Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other browsers, before those fixes were integrated in those downstream browsers. “This is patch-gap abuse,” the Edge team said . “The technique is not new, but the speed and expertise required is changing. AI-assisted analysis and exploit development could compress work that once took weeks into hours, increasing the chance that a usable exploit emerges while either exposure window remains open.” Researchers from Epoch AI recently used GLM 5.3 to emulate an unsophisticated attacker and target the Firefox patch gap. Using about $1,000 in API credits and as little as 12 hours of work per target, it compromised every Firefox release shipped between Sept. 17 and Oct. 26. “We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider,” the researchers wrote . In response, the Mozilla team has decided to take several actions to prevent patch gap abuse, for example by no longer releasing the regression tests associated with security fixes. “We’ve observed that GLM 5.3 is much less effective at patch-gapping when a regression test is not present, so we’ve reintroduced a practice of keeping these confidential until after the fix has shipped,” Firefox CTO Bobby Holley wrote . More diligence in patching, not less disclosure In a report last month dubbed PatchSlop, security firm Terra found that the rate of incomplete or broken fixes across open-source projects increased eightfold this year . “A patch that only blocks the reported input can give the impression the bug is addressed even if it’s still there in the underlying code,” the company’s researchers said. “It functions as a map for attackers, marking out both vulnerable code and what the defender thought the bug was. Looking just outside the diff (another encoding, another address range, another path into the same function) is one of the cheapest forms of bug hunting. We believe a growing share of attacker effort, and AI tokens, goes into exactly this.” The answer is not for open-source projects and software companies to hide vulnerability details and stop publishing security advisories, but to produce better patches. And some researchers believe this is possible, even when patching gets automated with the help of AI agents. In Rubrik’s case, after the company noticed that bugs it had marked as fixed kept coming back, Nejad’s team added its own variant hunting step that runs automatically in the pipeline after fixes are developed. The company began routing simple bugs to AI patching while reserving complex flaws, such as authentication bypasses, for human engineers. “Yes, attackers do have that context, but you have that context first, and you can act on that,” Nejad said. In a blog post this month , OpenAI noted that its Linux vulnerability research and patching pipeline needed iterative testing and variant analysis because initial patches “failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.” “We recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more,” the company’s researchers said. The Open Source Security Foundation’s guidance for AI-assisted patching also advises teams to “have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker” and Trail of Bits has released an agent skill that requires testing at least one distinct variant based on the bug’s root cause before a patch can be submitted. “It is clear there needs to be greater diligence and rigor when patching vulnerabilities,” Terra CEO Shahar Peled told CSO. “This means finding the root cause of any flaw, searching across the codebase for similar bugs and re-testing the system to ensure the patch itself doesn’t introduce a new vulnerability.”
summary: This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered. Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco.
