title: Government science advisers: ‘No framework for datacentre demand’
raw_text:
The UK has no agreed method for working out how much onshore datacentre capacity it needs, and delays in securing grid connections are a key factor in where new sites go.

That’s according to the Government Office for Science, which published a report of a meeting chaired by chief scientific adviser Angela McLean in February. The report represents “the combined views of roundtable participants” and is explicitly “not a statement of government policy” but does provide useful insight into the datacentre debate at national planning level.

According to the report, the group found “no obvious frameworks to determine how much onshore datacentre capacity the UK will need in the future”, and said demand was “very hard to estimate”. Sizing decisions should start from what UK capacity is essential – where offshore provision is not an option, it said – and from tasks datacentres perform across the economy, rather than from sector-by-sector demand.

“Water is not a major constraint on datacentre siting in the UK,” it said. The notes state that datacentres can be cooled without water using closed-loop systems and ventilation, given the UK’s climate, and that Amazon Web Services’ facilities reportedly run waterless for around 97% of the year. It notes the trade-off is power, and using less water means using more electricity.

The roundtable recommended the UK build a national interactive map of every datacentre, plotting sites alongside fibre routes, power lines and other infrastructure. The aim is to give developers, planners and communities a shared picture of where capacity sits, from hyperscale campuses down to small edge sites.

The notes draw a line between workloads that need to stay in the UK and those that do not. Regulated public services and industries under data protection rules such as GDPR generally require onshore sites, it said, and there are “strong arguments” for onshore capacity to serve national security and defence. Ultra-low-latency tasks – high-frequency trading and growing financial artificial intelligence (AI) use among them – also tie capacity to specific locations.

Much of the rest can go elsewhere, says the report. The notes say many workloads tolerate some latency or are not sensitive to data location, so they can use offshore facilities or, in future, centralised mega datacentres. They cite Ukraine’s experience of hostile actors as a reason to favour offshore or distributed capacity for resilience.

Grid connections are cited as a pinch point. The notes say delays in establishing a grid connection are a key factor in siting and “risk undermining the UK’s digital growth objectives”. They float removing the government requirement for new power generation to be connected to the grid as a way to cut delays and improve national resilience.

Planning is another gap identified. There is currently no national planning guidance for datacentre siting, and the notes point to strategies in the Netherlands and Saudi Arabia as references. They argue clearer guidance would give developers and communities more certainty, and that public acceptance depends on people seeing a national need, clear local benefits and developers they trust.

The timing coincides with lively debate decisions on planning, grid connections and datacentre location. 

The debate nationally lacks reliable figures. Computer Weekly analysis published this week has highlighted the dearth of reliable data around datacentre planning, in particular with regard to electricity draw, water use, and even the numbers of datacentres in existence and in the pipeline.

Computer Weekly has spent several months attempting to build reliable estimates. It has drawn on the Barbour ABI construction database and Energy Performance Certificate registers and found 88 verified existing UK datacentre sites with a combined capacity of about 1.6GW, against a committed pipeline of 173 schemes and about 14.6GW. The recommendation for a national map echoes that work. The numbers are contested because no shared, verified inventory exists.

Demand uncertainty runs through the meeting notes. The roundtable said future capacity would be variable and geographic, would depend on balance between small firms and large consumers, and would hinge on the pace of AI adoption – which itself depends on domestic datacentre capacity. It acknowledged that over-provisioning may be necessary to absorb that uncertainty, and that AI and non-AI services are already blurring as cloud sites evolve into combined general and AI facilities.

It acknowledged that workloads differ sharply. Training AI models is generally less latency-sensitive than running them, and for some large language models, demand has shifted from training to inference, which the notes say carries a significantly greater environmental impact at scale. Image processing for agriculture and transport is among the fastest-growing uses and typically needs localised capacity because of the volume of data involved.

Nine people took part in the roundtable. Alongside Angela McLean, the roundtable included Clive Richardson (Amazon Web Services), Dawn Childs (Pure Data Centres Group), Dimitra Simeonidou (University of Bristol), Eve Schooler (University of Oxford), John Booth (BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT), Luisa Cardani (TechUK), Patrick Devine-Wright (Exeter University) and Tim Watson (Loughborough University).

No grid or energy system operator sat at the table, and no water or planning regulator, even though grid delays and planning are two of the report’s central themes. The notes also carry the caution that they are advice, not a decision. The government has not committed to the map, to planning guidance or to changing grid connection rules.

The eight-month gap between meeting and publication points to a slow clearance loop in a fast-moving area. In that time, the UK pressed ahead with AI growth zones and datacentre planning decisions against capacity and demand figures that, by the advisers’ own account, nobody has a framework to test.

Waste heat and climate add further constraints. The notes say reuse needs datacentres sited near infrastructure that can use the heat, and that opportunities are limited without district heat networks and when sites sit on former industrial or greenfield land. Possible use cases include laundry, food preparation and greenhouses. Siting must also adapt to flooding, temperature and water availability.

title: Data dive: The UK datacentre numbers that don’t add up
raw_text:
The UK datacentre debate seems to run on a handful of numbers. There are 520 of them, or 500, or 450. Meanwhile, they are in the queue for 73GW (gigawatts) or 57.88GW of grid connections, and that translates to 315 datacentres.

They drink 6.6 million litres of water a day, which will soon be 19.8 million, or 14 million, or 42 million, depending on which paper you read. Each figure is put out there with great confidence. Almost none of them survive contact with evidence.

The numbers travel through the documents that steer policy. This includes written evidence to the Environmental Audit Committee, Ofgem consultations, Freedom of Information responses from the National Energy System Operator (NESO), and submissions from the water industry. From there, they pass into the Guardian, the Times, the Daily Mail and the BBC. By the time a council, a minister or a resident cites them, the trail back to the original data is cold.

Computer Weekly has spent months building a more forensic picture of the same territory, using the Barbour ABI construction database and the Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) registers to count what exists, what is planned and what it might draw.

This article traces the headline numbers to their source, tests them against that research, and asks why approximations keep getting reported as fact. The answers matter because these figures appear in influential publications, serve as ammunition for campaign groups, and make their way into documents submitted to Parliament, where decisions on planning, water and grid capacity are made against them.

The 500-datacentre illusion

The most repeated figure is the simplest, and the shakiest. The UK government’s own investment website tells overseas investors that Britain “hosts over 520 datacentres, the largest market in Western Europe”. TechUK put the count at 500 in its 2025 water report. The Guardian used 520 and 450 within days of each other. The range, 450 to 520, has hardened into a “fact” of the datacentre debate.

Our analysis of non-domestic EPC registers – which show the certificates every large building must have – found 57,026 large non-domestic properties, of which 229 scored as datacentre candidates. After checking each against planning records, operator directories and press reports, 88 stand up as confirmed existing sites, with 20 campus duplicates. Their combined capacity is about 1.6GW.

Meanwhile, the 450 to 520 range appears to be a count of buildings on commercial directories, not of verified sites. Data Center Map, the directory these counts are usually drawn from, now lists just over 600 UK facilities – but a directory entry is not a working datacentre, and many are single buildings on multi-building campuses, planned rather than live sites, or duplicates.

The EPC method has limits. It is a lower bound. It misses buildings under about 2,000m2 and very new sites that have not yet been certified. But it is built on energy performance certificates, not marketing content. The distance between “over 520” and roughly 90 verified sites is the gap between a directory entry and an actual datacentre.

TL;DR – The datacentre numbers that don’t add up

  • The “520 datacentres” claim traces to a directory count; EPC-based counting confirms fewer than 100 substantial sites, roughly 1.6GW in total.
  • The 73GW and 315-project grid queue is a register of speculative positions, not a construction pipeline; committed capacity in planning is about 14.6GW.
  • Water UK’s 6.6 million litres-a-day figure rests on self-reported ranges from 73 sites, extrapolated to 500 – precision the underlying data cannot support.
  • Affinity Water’s “125 proposed datacentres” produced three actual planning applications.
  • The claim that datacentres use 2.5% of UK electricity, rising fourfold by 2030, rests on a committee chair’s framing; analysis of DESNZ data puts the 2024 share at 1.8%.

A queue, not a pipeline

While the datacentre count inflates what exists, the grid queue inflates what’s coming. Ofgem’s July consultation stated that “around 73GW across approximately 315 projects” of datacentre demand sits in the connection queue. The Guardian repeated those numbers, and upgraded them all to “hyperscale datacentres”. The figures read like a forecast, but they are not.

The first problem is provenance. The 73GW is not Ofgem’s invention – it is NESO’s own figure, rounded up. NESO’s written evidence to the Environmental Audit Committee states that “new pipeline data collected in 2025 from distribution and transmission network operators shows around 72.8GW of connection requests through to 2039”, which it says is “a huge step change in demand in the sector”.

Of that, nearly 59GW sits at transmission level (the high-voltage national grid) and the remainder on the regional distribution networks (lower-voltage local grids). NESO’s transmission figure is the part it will stand behind – 57.88GW in its FOI response.

Asked to account for the distribution portion, NESO told Computer Weekly: “As we don’t own the distribution data, we can’t verify these numbers.” So, the headline number rests partly on a distribution figure that the body which published it now says it cannot verify.

Ofgem’s press office went further. Its July 2026 press release that announced the reforms said demand connection applications “have surged from 41GW to 125GW, in under a year. This rise is driven largely by datacentre projects, accounting for at least 80GW”. Asked how those figures were reached, Ofgem told Computer Weekly they “were provided to Ofgem by NESO” – an 80GW figure NESO has never published, and 7GW above the 72.8GW total it did publish.

The second problem is how the data is characterised. Asked how the “nearly 59GW” was derived, NESO said in an FOI response that it holds a dataset of “transmission connected demand” with an “assigned technology type”, and that it “carried out internal analysis in order to identify what we believe to be the datacentres within this dataset. This is where the figure of 59GW has been calculated from”.

Some judgement is unavoidable – there is no official register, and our own count is an inference too – but the difference is in how it is disclosed. NESO published no method, no thresholds and no project-level breakdown until FOI requests drew them out. And the numbers change between its documents without stated reconciliation. Its parliamentary evidence, drawn from 2025 pipeline data, puts “nearly 59GW” at transmission level with “40 of the 173 projects” between 500MW and 1,500MW, while its October 2026 FOI response gives 57.88GW across 164 projects, 36 of them in that band.

The third problem is what we consider a queue actually amounts to. Connection applications are positions reserved by developers, not schemes with planning consent, finance or a customer. Our Barbour ABI analysis finds 173 projects, totalling about 14.6GW, that have entered the planning system and are not yet built. That is real money and real land, and it is barely a fifth of the 73GW headline, which looks more like a ledger of options that will never be exercised.

Water: Precision built on buckets

The water numbers carry a great deal of weight too, because they were also placed directly before Parliament. On 2 April 2026, Water UK told the Environmental Audit Committee that “datacentres currently use approximately 6.6 million litres of water per day”, rising to 19.8 million if the government’s plan to triple capacity by 2030 holds. The figures have since been repeated by the Guardian, the Times and the BBC, and by campaign groups keen to show the thirst of the datacentre build-out.

Footnote 16 of that submission explains the method. The figure, it says, is “Water UK analysis based on a sample size of 116 datacentres (almost a quarter of the estimated 500 datacentres in the UK – see TechUK (2025))”, and “was extrapolated out from the sample to estimate the whole sector’s usage”.

The “TechUK (2025)” report referred to can be read here, and the “500 datacentres” cited by Water UK is likely the upper figure of the “450 to 500” on page 9. Here, we are directed to a footnote that points towards a previous TechUK report that contains no reference to the number of datacentres in the UK.

When we asked how its figure was built, Water UK first said: “We didn’t use TechUK figures for datacentre water use.” It then explained that the estimate was “based on how much water the water companies supplied to datacentres from a sample, which was then extrapolated out to meet the number in the report – 500 datacentres”, but did not attribute a source. By its final email, the 500 was again “taken from the TechUK report”.

However you read that, any pretence at precision is unsupported. TechUK’s survey, run with the Environment Agency, drew 80 responses and 73 usable sites – not 116 – and it did not collect precise figures.

It said: “Sites that did [measure] were asked to select their average annual consumption from a set of ranges.” These buckets were “less than 1,000m³, 1,000-10,000m³, 10,001-100,000m³, and more than 100,000m³”. It added: “We collected annual consumption in ranges rather than exact figures.” No totals were produced.

Those ranges are enormous. The two middle buckets each span a factor of 10. The top bucket has no ceiling. A site logged as “more than 100,000m³” could be 100,000 or 2,000,000. And because water use is intensely skewed – the MOSL/WRc study found six sites accounted for 65% of the sector’s consumption – the national total is really a statement about a handful of buildings in the widest, open-ended range. To reach a precise 6.6 million litres a day, someone has to assume where each site sits. Water UK has not published those assumptions.

The metered market tells a calmer story. MOSL, which runs England’s non-household water market, estimates datacentres use about 1.9 billion litres a year, or roughly 0.2% of non-household consumption. Water companies lose about three billion litres a day to leaks.

The gap between projection and reality is stark elsewhere too, and adds to the evidence against unverified queue figures.

Affinity Water, which serves a region that includes datacentre hotspot Slough, told MPs that “approximately 125 datacentres are either proposed or under construction” in its area. That figure came from planning database Glenigans, it said, but we have no idea how the data was filtered. When Affinity tracked which of those 125 reached the planning process, the answer was three.

“Only three have come through to actual proposals, or actual planning applications,” its public affairs adviser, Richard Emmott, told Computer Weekly.

The Guardian ran with the 125 figure. Meanwhile, the Affinity submission to Parliament also talked of “some individual facilities requesting supplies of up to 35 litres per second, equivalent to the peak water demand of 3,500 homes.” The Daily Mail and Huffington Post ran with that figure.

Affinity Water’s Emmott told Computer Weekly that the 35 litres per second request was a peak demand projection for firefighting purposes. He also said the datacentre demand Affinity can verify is “less than one megalitre per day”, which contrasts with 950 megalitres of daily supply.

Computer Weekly has already shown how a single misread figure can distort the water debate. In that case, a report by the Government Digital Sustainability Alliance (GDSA) looked in detail at water consumption associated with artificial intelligence (AI) and datacentres, and made an established fact of a “five billion litres a day” shortfall by 2050 when it is actually the worst-case scenario in the Environment Agency’s planning. The best case – assuming infrastructure improvements – shows a surplus.

These numbers come in many cases from submissions to Parliament. A trade body that puts a precise figure to a select committee should be held to it. There is public interest in reporting the kind of discrepancies we find here, because of the effect they can have on datacentre planning and public opinion.

Electricity draw: What we know, what we don’t

The figures cited for datacentre electricity use also come with some uncertainty. In a 16 April 2026 notice launching a Science, Innovation and Technology Committee inquiry, its chair, Dame Chi Onwurah, wrote that “datacentres currently use about 2.5% of the UK’s electricity, but their consumption is expected to rise fourfold by 2030”. It was a framing remark at an inquiry launch into an uncertain question, not a finding.

Measured against our research on datacentre electricity, the 2.5% figure overstates, and the projected rise is just that – a projection with no apparent calculation we can examine. Our analysis of Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) data finds UK datacentres used 1.8% of Great Britain’s grid electricity in 2024, up from 1.2% in 2020 – the most recent published breakdown that separates datacentres out.

That is now two years old, and the estate has grown since, so today’s true share will be higher. The open question is, how much higher? The fourfold projection to 10% by 2030 is where the trouble lies – a committed pipeline of roughly nine times the existing estate makes the direction plausible, but the specific figure rests on a capacity trajectory with no published details.

Why the numbers inflate

Each distortion in the numbers has a beneficiary.

The circa 500 datacentre count serves companies that sell property and investment intelligence, as well as trade bodies that benefit from appearing to be at the centre of a boom.

The grid queue numbers are populated by a place in line that is currently a cheap option for a developer – easy to hold, easy to abandon – and all calculated to help attract investment. For Ofgem, NESO and the network operators, the worst-case figure such activities generate is a lever that helps justify commitment fees and queue reforms, and strengthens the case for investment in the network.

Water use estimates serve an industry under pressure to justify investment, and campaign groups for whom a bigger number drives urgency.

Journalists, who use what are essentially lobby-supplied figures, can only presume an editorial line driven by politics. But the result is to undermine the scrutiny journalists exist to apply. When an ostensibly progressive paper repeats a trade body’s estimate as fact, the number acquires a weight in Westminster that its data never earned.

How we built our numbers

Our figures on the existing datacentre estate and those in the planning process come from two datasets, and both carry limits we state openly. The existing estate is inferred from non-domestic EPC registers. Of 57,026 large non-domestic buildings, 229 scored as datacentre candidates, and 88 survived manual verification. Capacity is published in megawatts where a site discloses it, but otherwise modelled from floor area – around 1,166W per square metre for colocation and 800W for enterprise. It is an estimated lower bound, not a metered load.

The pipeline is drawn from data from Barbour ABI, a construction planning tracking service. We count as “active” only projects that have entered the planning system and are not yet built. The most recent count made 173 schemes, and about 14.6GW. Capacity is taken from the project text where stated, modelled from floor area where not, estimated from trade and press reports in a few cases, while 28 schemes carry no megawatt figure and are excluded from the capacity total. We do not count “pre-planning” announcements as part of the pipeline.

These methods are imperfect. What sets them apart from the public numbers is that they are published, reproducible and open to challenge.

Reliable planning needs reliable numbers

The datacentre build-out is real, and its demands on water and power are serious enough to justify hard questions. But the debate has settled on a set of numbers that are often quite unreliable – a datacentre marketing directory presented as built reality, a queue of options presented as a committed pipeline, self-reported ranges presented as a precise national figure, and a committee chair’s aside presented as a finding. Each flatters the case of whoever is citing it, but almost all collapse when traced to their source.

Until someone publishes a datacentre demand forecast with a stated baseline, a transparent method and a confidence range, the planning, water and grid decisions now being taken will rest on numbers that cannot bear their weight. Britain may well need datacentres, but it cannot afford to build them on figures it can’t defend.

summary:
The UK datacentre debate seems to run on a handful of numbers. There are 520 of them, or 500, or 450. Meanwhile, they are in the queue for 73GW (gigawatts) or 57.88GW of grid connections, and that translates to 315 datacentres.

They drink 6.6 million litres of water a day, which will soon be 19.8 million, or 14 million, or 42 million, depending on which paper you read. Each figure is put out there with great confidence.
